subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was going on to another subject, but I shall do so at another time.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I am sadly in need of the lessons, both in finance and in poker, that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and other members of the house this afternoon. I do not know how much the minister is in need of the lessons in poker, but I am in need of them and I am grateful to the previous speaker for them. As to the lessons in finance, possibly the minister and I can both give them what is called in parliamentary language, due consideration.
The Minister of Finance is a notable figure in any House of Commons, possibly the most important after the Prime Minister. Most of what he does is in fact less subject to scrutiny than what is done by his colleagues. Finance is not something apart from policy, in reality it is an expression of policy. The Minister of Finance has told the house, that many hundreds of millions of dollars are required to carry out the government's policies during the fiscal year 1946-1947. He alone is not responsible for the amount. In criticizing a budget one is not criticizing the Minister of Finance alone, he is criticizing the policy which has made necessary the raising of such sums of money. Sometimes it happens that one does not criticize the amount itself but is critical of the way in which it is intended to be raised.
It is difficult in the second week of a debate of this kind, a debate which has followed so closely in the wake of public consideration of many questions which were discussed by the minister in the dominion-provincial conference, to say very much that has not already been said. The minister has pointed out that he has prepared his budget on the assumption that no general agreement with the provinces could be .had, and he said that his task has been made extremely difficult by the fact that no general agreement was reached with the provinces. He has told

The Budget-Mr. Hackett
the house that because no general agreement was reached he intends to seek special and private agreements with the various provinces. I note that in the speech from the throne the following appears:
A meeting of the coordinating committee of the dominion-provincial conference was held in January. Progress was made in the consideration ot proposals submitted by the dominion and provincial governments. The committee will meet again on April 25.
As a result of the conference, there may be further legislative proposals.
Surely the legislation then contemplated was not the enactment of the budget resolutions.
I shall deal almost exclusively with this one aspect of the budget, the intention of the government to make private and individual agreements with, the provinces. In substance the government intends to say to each province: "If you will desist from collecting taxes we will pay you a large amount of money. If you, the provinces, will not levy and collect taxes on personal incomes, will not levy and collect taxes on corporations, will not levy and collect taxes on successions or inheritances, we will pay you a large sum of money." I am not mentioning some of the details of that offer, because I wish to deal with the general proposition. That is what the government says to the provinces. And it says, "Furthermore we, the dominion government, as a return for that concession, will pay you $15 a head for your population as determined by the census of 1941 or at a later date; we will guarantee that that payment will be at least 50 per cent greater than the payments made to you under the wartimes agreements; and we will furthermore undertake to increase these payments as your population increases and as your production per capita increases."
The minister has placed on record a table which shows approximately what this means. It shows- that the amount guaranteed als a minimum if all the provinces accept the proposal is $181 million, that it is likely to be $198 million per annum, and then of course there is the possibility and even the probability of increase.
I want to say here that I am not adverse to assistance being given to provinces, assistance based on need, and my party is not adverse to that principle. What I object to is the method by which it is sought to administer that assistance, and it is to that method and its result that I intend to direct my remarks this afternoon.
I do not understand that any province is adverse to a method whereby need may be taken into consideration in a reallocation of 63260-218
the revenues of the country. I find at page 221 of the records of the plenary session of the dominion-provincial conference this utterance by the premier of Quebec:
The federal proposals are unacceptable for the very many reasons I have given and which it would be unnecessary to repeat. As stated by me the door is left open-if I may say so without offence to anyone-for Ottawa to come to a better sense of proportion. The door is left open for friendly cooperation and understanding, based upon the fundamentals of the constitution and taking into account the past, the present and the future.
At the time of confederation the chief sources of revenues were customs duties and excise taxes. They were indirect taxes, and they were allocated to the dominion. Since then, changes have taken place, and direct taxes, to which the provinces were restricted, have become a greater source of revenue, greater by far than the indirect taxe3 to which the dominion resorted at the time of confederation. I believe that these facts should be taken into consideration. I see no objection to a reallocation of the revenues available for purposes of government. But I do object, and I object with all the sincerity and with all the vehemence that I can command, to the methods by which it is proposed to bring about that reallocation. And here are some of my objections.
The province of Quebec, for instance, has an annual budget of something under $100 million : under this proposal it would receive from the dominion government just under $60 million a year. The province of Ontario has a budget of about $100 million, and under this arrangement it would receive something like $65 million a year. My suggestion is this, that we have received a constitution, and part of that constitution is parliamentary, representative and responsible government. At every moment of every day a government stands poised on the confidence of the house and of the people of the province or the dominion. It is the duty of government to raise the moneys which are required for the purposes of government. It is the duty of government to account to the house for every last penny that is raised and spent for purposes of government.
It is there that we find that the genius of those from whom we descend has expressed itself. It is in that series of balances and checks that a form of government has been evolved which gives protection to the property owner, and meets the needs of those who are in distress.
Now, what is the result here? We would find a province receiving, in the two instances that I have mentioned, something like sixty or possibly more, per cent of its revenues as-I

The Budget-Mr. Hackett

was'going to say-a hand-out. These governments would be receiving it from an agency to which they would owe no responsibility whatever; they would be getting it, not from those whom they had taxed, but from someone to whom they owed no duty to account. That would mean extravagance. Money from home is always money easily spent, and money that has come to one from a friend or money that one finds is never accounted for with the same care that is exercised in accounting for that which has cost effort to get.
Then we come to the other side of the medal. Here in this house there would be at least $200 million a year for which nobody would be accountable. The Minister of Finance would rise in his place and say, "I have paid $200 million to the provinces" and we would have to say, "how' nice." If we asked how much of that money had been wasted in one province or another he could give no answer. There would be no check upon waste. This proposal is entirely subversive of our whole parliamentary system. Moreover, I submit, though I have been unable to find any case absolutely in point, that this proposal is entirely unconstitutional. Where is there in our constitution anything that permits the government of a province for instance, using the colourful language of the Minister of Finance, to lease a field of taxation, to sell a right of taxation? Where is there anything that entitles the government of a province to barter away its right of taxation, or a province or the dominion its duty to account to those from whom it collects the money?
I have scrutinized the British North America Act very carefully and I can find nothing in any of the subsections of section 91, which contains the powers of the dominion, and I can find nothing in the subsections of section 92, which contains the powers of the province, that warrants such an undertaking. Furthermore, wherever there is any intimation of one legislative body impinging upon the field of the other, it is very carefully and specifically stated. For instance, if one turns to section 94, which has to do with the common law in the provinces other than Quebec, one finds that it is competent to the dominion to enact legislation imposing the common law upon any of the provinces other than Quebec. That is a privilege of the dominion, but it is conditioned upon the province which is affected by such legislation passing concurrent legislation. One also finds that where the judges are appointed and paid by the federal authority, and where they come under the control, discipline and organizing power of the province, it is specifically laid down in the act that such divided jurisdiction obtains.
fMr. Hackett.]
Further, we find in section 12-I think that is the section where all the powers which at one time were vested in the legislatures which preceded confederation, or which were conferred upon them by imperial statute were handed on to the parliament of Canada-that in none of the subsections is there anything that suggests a right whereby the dominion should purchase or enter into an agreement under which the constitutional function of a province should cease in order that the dominion might have greater taxing power than it would otherwise have.
It is perhaps of interest at this point to refer to the constitution of Australia, because in that country, under article 51, which is the counterpart of section 91 of our constitution, there does exist a right which would warrant, justify, enable and permit a transaction of this kind. It is foupd in subsection 37 of article 51 and is in these terms:
Matters referred to the parliament of the commonwealth by the parliament or parliaments of any state or states, but so that the law shall extend only to states by whose parliaments the matter is referred or which afterwards adopt the law.
So we are embarking upon a course which is entirely new. We are embarking upon a course for which there is no direct legislative authority. We are embarking upon a course which no one would ever have thought of until the great necessities for money which are now upon us were felt. It is interesting to note how this tendency to increase the amount of money which is levied by this parliament, and which escapes the scrutiny of the house, is growing. On turning to the estimates for 1947, one finds that in a total budget of something like $1,566 million, something like $876 million is authorized by statute, of which $580 million represents interest on our obligations, while $285 million is charged to the Department of National Health and Welfare and includes cost of legislation which was enacted about a year ago.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And family allowances and old age pensions.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And family allowances and old age pensions. I point out the tendency to increase these statutory amounts which, like the salaries of judges and officials, are beyond the power of this house to criticize effectively or to control at all. And here I want to make a point which I think may have escaped the attention of some. In 1937 a royal commission was set up, frequently referred to as the Rowell-Sirois commission. It is the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. At that time the

The Budget-Mr. Hackett
necessities which brought about the most useful examination of these problems were almost exclusively the necessities of a few provinces which had not sufficient revenue from direct taxation-especially since the invasion of the field by the dominion authorities-to carry on their governmental activities with any degree of comfort. The situation is now quite changed. While there is still a need for reallocation of the taxable revenue of Canada at large, the most necessitous of all these agencies is the dominion government. The one which cannot wait, the one which is insistent is the dominion. A strange aspect of the budget is this. In the royal commission report it was suggested that a reallocation of revenues might become necessary, and one finds the following at page 72 of the second volume of the report:
One of the difficulties inherent irr any federal system is the rigidity which marks the division of jurisdiction between the central and local governments.
A little farther along we find the following:
Our instructions obviously contemplated the suitability of a reallocation of powers which would require constitutional amendments, and we are reporting as to what in our opinion will "conduce to a more efficient, independent and economical discharge of governmental responsibility in Canada."
Then farther on they say:
We desire merely to emphasize the necessity that some procedure for constitutional change should be evolved.
We think that the introduction of a measure of flexibility in the Canadian federal system should be considered. A number of provinces may on occasion be willing and may even actively desire the dominion to assume responsibility for a function which is beyond its constitutional powers. The dominion may itself be willing to assume the function but be unable to do so until public opinion has developed to the extent of permitting a constitutional amendment to be made.
I point out that it was at all times understood there could be nothing in the nature of a reallocation of revenues similar to those mentioned in the budget until there had been a constitutional amendment. To-day it is said an amendment is not necessary. It is well to remember that the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations made its report before the war. When the war came, agreements between the provinces and the dominion were entered into, and the dominion is now in possession of these so-called fields of taxation; the dominion is in possession of the territory.
In passing I may say, as an interesting feature, that the dominion was given these rights to tax for a definite period and for the purpose of winning the war, and that at a certain moment the dominion government diverted the proceeds of these rights to tax 63260-2184
from the purpose of winning the war to the purposes of winning an election, which just shows one of the difficulties which will ensue from the prosecution of this centralizing policy. But let us go on. Under these agreements the dominion has the exclusive right for a time, and I am sure that my hon. friends will not argue that because under the peace, order and good government enactments of section 91 they were given, as a result, and because of the emergency arising out of the war, the right to occupy the provincial field, that right remains in them for any additional period. I believe that has been established by the passage of the legislation in December last when the transitional emergency was born. We produce emergencies with greater facility than we used to. It was never intimated, never suggested, that these powers whereby the dominion would exclusively collect moneys by direct taxation would remain. I am aware that judgments of highest authority have held that the dominion has the right to levy taxes of all types, direct and indirect. Nevertheless these private agreements which the dominion offers to the provinces-one by one-go farther. They would result in the suspension of the most considerable, the most elementary, the most fundamental function of government, namely, that of levying taxes and being called upon to account for them. But the dominion is in possession of the field. It collects from income and corporation taxes something like SI,550 million. The minister has said somewhere that he thinks it should be reduced to $1,200 million, because of some changes that are about to become effective; nevertheless there are SI,200 million, without considering succession duties, which the dominion seeks. It is going to spend these amounts and from them it undertakes to give the provinces about $200 million a year. It is going to do all this without amending or attempting to amend in any way the British North America Act.
Speaking at the plenary session of the dominion-provincial conference, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, as reported at page 9 of the proceedings:
In all its proposals, the dominion has assumed that Canada's federal system of government should be preserved and strengthened. I should like to repeat what I said at the plenary session on August 6, last.
I skip a bit, and continue:
The only constitutional change suggested is the proposal, already mentioned, for the delegation of powers, and with this one exception under which the dominion is prepared to enlarge the powers of the provinces, none of the dominion proposals would require an amendment to the British North America Act, or involve any fundamental disturbance of the
The Budget-Mr. Hackett

traditional pattern of confederation. In this unsettled period of world transition, it would be unwise to seek constitutional change, or to make irrevocable commitments. What we are now seeking is to meet urgent needs, on a temporary basis, by the simplest and most effective means.
To say that the constitution of the dominion may be so completely perverted, so completely uprooted, and to refer to it as a mere passing event reminds one of those incidents to which the newspapers gave some notoriety a few years ago, and which I believe they called trial * marriages. The provinces cannot undergo for three or five years the experience of the type outlined by the minister and survive; the integrity of the fiscal organization of any individual province could never be revived. We know now the great difficulty the dominion is experiencing in returning to the provinces those exclusive rights it derived from them for the purpose and the period of the war. I think it fair to assume that if the federal government obtain these exclusive taxing rights for a period of five years they never will be returned to the provinces.
I want to make one further statement, and I hope my hon. friends will not think I am attempting to be unnecessarily disagreeable. My province has been torn and victimized for twenty-five years by a fear of something called conscription. The good people of that province were told-and if anyone here is anxious to hear what was said I have the newspaper clippings-that they owed no service in wars overseas; and they were told that upon the highest authority. As a result of that policy which was preached in one province but not in others, a parliamentary majority was obtained and maintained in this house for twenty-five years by hon. gentlemen opposite. War came and the nation was torn asunder. I pray that now hon. gentlemen opposite will not attempt in the economic field to convert the necessities of those provinces which at the moment have not the wealth which enables them to draw, from direct taxation, the moneys they need for their maintenance and self-support, into a party advantage. I ask that an end be put to dividing in order that one may rule. If it be competent to the minister and the government to make a special trade with a friendly province; if it be competent to go to a province and enter into an agreement which will deny it the power to tax and the power to scrutinize, I ask, what would happen to that province which happened to be in opposition to the party in power, whether it be the party now in power or another party, if that party should not like the economic doctrines or the political creed of the needy province? We all remember the day when
rMr. Hackett.]
something was said that there was not a five-cent piece for a Tory province. Much as I dislike referring to that incident, because I do not believe the statement was meant, it does show to what extremities a government might go to starve a recalcitrant province into submission if the pernicious doctrine enunciated by the minister were admitted.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do not want to cover the ground that has been covered already by my colleagues, but I agree with them that the exemptions in the lower income tax brackets are far from satisfactory. I welcome the consideration the minister has shown the fishermen and farmers in allowing them to average their incomes over a three-year period. That is only a partial step; but it is in the right direction.
There is one phase of the income tax to which I had hoped the minister would give some considerable thought, a matter I have brought to his attention before. On the farm the whole family works as one unit; yet when the income tax return must be made up the tax is levied only on the one income, that of the farmer. Previously the minister pointed out to me that other women and other families work, as well as the farmer's wife and family, but again I should like to draw his attention to the fact that the farmer's wife and family contribute more to his income than is the case in any other business. I do not want to elaborate on this point, or go into details, but generally speaking the farmer's wife adds more to the income of the farm than in any other case that can be cited. The same can be said of the farmer's family, who increase the income of the farm by their efforts in connection with milking, haying, harvesting, feeding live stock and the many other chores around the farm. But when the income tax

The Budget-Mr. Bryce
form is filled out, the income of the whole family is reckoned as the farmer's income, and it is taxed as such. I should like the minister to give attention to this point and see if there is not some other way of granting relief where the entire family produces the income that is taxed.
I wish to go on record as endorsing what the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) said regarding cooperatives. I do not want to repeat his argument, but I want the minister to know that I am wholeheartedly in support of what the hon. member said.
I regret that in this budget the government, through the minister's department is forcing the cooperatives into a profitmaking class, by this three per cent return on capital investment. The minister is classing two different things together in his taxation, two things which should be separated, namely joint stock companies and cooperative societies. One is a service for profit and the other is a service at cost. You can mix them, just as you mix oil and water; but they will not stay mixed. They are entirely different, and represent two different ways of doing business.
I was born in a cooperative home. I have been a cooperator all my life, and I cannot help thinking at this time that in putting cooperatives in this position the Minister of Finance is trying to destroy the principles for which they were formed.

I agree with what the minister has said, and with Your Honour's observations. However, to support my argument I shall read the contrast. It is as follows:
The Contrasting Features of a Joint S'tock Company and a Cooperative Society
A Joint Stock Corporation
1.	Is a union of capital as an investment to earn a profit.
2.	Shareholding may be anonymous; shares are freely transferable and may be held by anyone.
3.	Is limited (as a general proposition) in the number of persons owning the business,
i.e., the shares are limited in number.
A Cooperative
1.	Is a union of persons to supply themselves with goods and services at cost.
2.	Shares are identified by persons; the shareholder must be admitted to membership or transfers must be approved by the board of directors.
3.	There is no limit to the number of persons who may participate in the business within its range of operations, i.e., the number of shares is not limited.
The Budget-Mr. Bryce

The Contrasting Features of a Joint Stock A Joint Stock Corporation-Con.
4.	The shares being limited in number they will fluctuate in value according to the profits they earn.
5.	Control by the individual is determined by the number of shares he holds.
6.	Surplus earnings, i.e., profits, are the property of the corporation.
7.	Surplus is divided among the shareholders on the basis of the number of shares held.
8.	No limit to the dividend paid on share capital.
9.	The joint stock company does business in a general way with the public; the buyers and sellers (the parties to the business transactions) are distinct and different.
10.	The selling price is normally above cost price and the surplus constitutes a trading profit.
11.	Business is done for the express purpose of realizing the trading profit which becomes the property of the corporation.
That is the difference between the two methods of doing business. Here to-day we have a discussion going on as to whether pools are cooperatives, or whether they are not. We have no yardstick to go by. We have no dominion cooperatives act. The government of to-day-and those of the past, both Liberal and Conservative-have failed to say what a cooperative is, and to-day we have people in doubt.
The minister says, in his budget, that the pools are subject to taxation for 1944 and 1S945. There seems to have been a great deal of doubt about this. Had the government brought in a cooperative act there would be no doubt at this time.
I understand that a cooperative bill was introduced in this house in 1906 and referred to a special committee. It seems to have been received favourably at that time, because a special committee of the house was set up to look into it. In the Journals of the House of Commons, volume 62, for 1906-1907, I find on pages 70 and 71 the evidence given before the committee by Mr. Mackenzie King, then deputy minister of labour, who was a witness before the committee. From his remarks I quote the following:
Leading economists of to-day both in England and the United States, men who have not at heart the interests of one class of society as against^ another, but who look impartially upon economic affairs, are pretty 'well one in the favour with which they view the cooperative movement as a movement exceptionally bene-

In the election campaign of 1911 the leaders of both parties promised cooperative legislation. To-day the organized farmers and cooperatives are still demanding a dominion cooperative act. Who will suffer the most? The farmer's wife and the farmer's children are going to suffer again. subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To continue from where I left off before supper, perhaps I should touch on some material I have received from the Winnipeg grain exchange; at least it came in one of their envelopes, containing a number of advertisements, which appeared in the western papers, prepared by the grain exchange and putting their point of view before the farming population of Canada.
The first advertisement says, "Who dares speak for Mr. Prairie Farmer?" Well, I can assure hon. members that I have been speaking for the prairie farmer in Manitoba for twenty-five years. I have always spoken on his behalf, both when I was on the farm and when I was president of the Manitoba federation of agriculture, and to-day as member for Selkirk I am still speaking for the farmer. I have nothing but the good and the prosperity of the Canadian farmer at heart, and I am sure that the rest of my days will be spent in working for the advancement of the farmer.
The first advertisement outlines wheat prices in the United States and at Fort William, the two .main trading centres. It says,
"You get less than $1.55 in Canada. The United States farmer gets $2.18 a bushel for his wheat." I do not think very much of this argument. The grain exchange omitted to tell our farmers that the United States price must conform to the ceiling set by the United States authorities; it is said to be related to the American formula for parity with the things the United States farmer has to buy, and it cannot be considered a world price. Taking the general necessaries of life, the common things we need to buy, I think everybody will agree that a Canadian bushel of wheat at $1.55 will buy as much in Canada as a United States bushel of wheat at $2.18 will buy in the United States. No doubt the grain' exchange or some individual can point out that automobiles and oil are cheaper in the United States; but if we take the necessaries of life which the farmer has to buy for his own family, the one bushel of wheat will buy as much as the other.
It is claimed by the Winnipeg grain exchange that the open market would bring the price of wheat up to the United States price, which they claim is the world price. I do not agree with that. Let us look at our experience of the past when the open market prevailed. Two years after the beginning of the war, to be exact, on February 2, 1942, hon. members will find that the Winnipeg May price was eighty cents and the Chicago May price was $1.29.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can you tell?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By the papers of that day.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With the grain exchange operating?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A difference of approximately fifty cents. It is really only forty-nine cents, but there were fractions, and I am not quite clear what the fractions were. If the argument of this advertisement is of any value, why at that time was there a fifty cent spread? And the Winnipeg grain exchange did nothing about it when they had an open market to work on.
In the Searle grain report of Wednesday, April 13, 1946, it says, "The exchange does not make the price"; so why bring this argument in, and flood western Canada with it, when with an open market we could get no more for our grain?
I have been an advocate of a wheat board which could guarantee a steady price from year to year so that the farmer knows what he is going to get for his produce. In any other industry the person who has something to sell takes into consideration, in setting the
The Budget-Mr. Bryce

selling price of his product, the cost of production plus a reasonable return for his labour. The farmer was forced to take what the grain exchange was willing to give him.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was left after the grain exchange got theirs, you mean.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right. He has had to sell his product in a market controlled by someone else and to buy the necessaries of life in a market controlled by someone else. There are many hon. members who remember the great demand by the private grain trade after the last world war that the wheat board be discontinued, and the farmer allowed to get the price to which he was entitled.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the same cry in 1932.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The same cry to-day by the same people. When the grain exchange came into the open market in August, 1920, wheat was $2.73 a bushel. But let us look at October of the following year; wheat was back down to $1.09. What benefit was the open market to us in those days? None whatever. Had the wheat board been continued, we at least would have had a steady price and an equal price for everybody instead of a fluctuating market.
Then, coming to December 16, 1932, with the open market still in full control, wheat dropped to the lowest record on record, 38| cents, on the Winnipeg market. It has been stated that this was the lowest price for wheat in 400 years. And the Winnipeg grain exchange, which was enjoying am open market, could do nothing about it. No doubt that is when they found out that the grain exchange does not set the .price.
Coming back to the advertisement again, it says, "Will you be satisfied with $1.25 for your wheat?" This statement was challenged and corrected by the press on June 19; but the grain exchange people and the private trade kept on using it because, no doubt, it suited their propaganda. Let me read to the house the statement of H. H. Hannam, president of the Canadian federation of agriculture, issued to the press on June 19:
On returning to Ottawa I am amazed to learn that reports which are entirely erroneous have been circulated in Canada during our absence, about the stand taken by the Canadian delegation while attending the recent international farmers' conference in London.
One statement at hand referring to the price of wheat says "the delegation stated that western farmers are prepared to accept a minimum wheat price on a long time contract at $1 a bushel with a maximum of $1.25." This statement is so completely untrue that it is ridiculous. 
No member of the Canadian delegation at any time suggested a long time contract at $1 a bushel or a maximum price of $1.25 a bushel.
In the official presentation from our delegation to the conference, reference was made to the wheat price programme purely to illustrate the pointy that Canadian farmers will support the principle of a stabilized price on a long time basis, but no mention whatever was made of any price per bushel in that statement. And the statement was read to the conference without supplementary comment.
To answer the question further, "Will you be satisfied with Si.25 a bushel?" may I say that we have been forced to take a lot less in times past when the grain exchange was in full control.
In the future surpluses will become necessary reserves for the food and agriculture organization. If we ever have surpluses, let us trust our farmers' organizations and the Canadian wheat board, and not the Winnipeg grain exchange, which has failed us in the past.
Further down, this advertisement says that even the British farmer got $1.78 for his wheat this year and that the French farmer was guaranteed $1.78. Let us look at this. The Canadian farmer sells his wheat at Fort William for $1.55 a bushel. It takes approximately twenty cents a bushel to take it to seaboard; that is Montreal or Halifax. So that makes $1.75 for the wheat at seaboard, and to equal the British or the French farmer's price it has to be taken across the ocean for three cents. It must be obvious to any unprejudiced person, or any person who has any sympathy for the people in the countries that have suffered so much, that the price we are receiving over there must be around $1.90, or about all that they can possibly be expected to pay.
We can hope that negotiations now under way will announce a price suitable to both parties; and while agreements may be bilateral for the time being, it will ultimately lead to an international agreement. We must adopt the principles of the united nations food and agricultural organization whose policy is to live and let others live too, sharing the food of a bounteous world.
The grain exchange was opened in 1903 and had a laudable object in view in those days. That was a place where men went to sell wheat and other men went to buy. But that was in 1903 and we have made vast strides since then. The method, while suitable in 1903, is far from being suitable to-day. A farmer who might go and cut wheat to-day with a reaper as in 1903 would be laughed at. He does not do that. He goes with a combine to-day. He is employing more modern ways of harvesting his crop. But the grain exchange is still the same 1903 machine.

The Budget-Mr. Bryce
Operations on the grain exchange are closed now because they failed to function or were not needed during the war years. During the first war the wheat board was needed because the grain exchange system was found wanting. In the hungry thirties, when the price went to 384 cents, there were cries all over the country to reestablish the wheat board, and again in the critical years of the second war the wheat board had to be made the sole marketing agency, since the out-of-date grain exchange system was not needed and could not fill the bill.
The wheat board has proved to be a modern way of marketing grain. Why go back to the old method now? In the forty years that the Winnipeg grain exchange has existed, I would point out to hon. members that there have been eighteen commissions in all which have sat and inquired into its operations. I know many hon. members admit that, but point out that the commissions never found anything wrong. But I am sure that When an organization needs a commission appointed approximately once in every two or three years to inquire into its business, there is an impression that something is very wrong; and looking over those commissions which have sat over the last forty years one asks who sat on them and how many farmers were on them. Had there been some bona fide farmers on those commissions, I am sure that some of the conclusions arrived at would have been much different.
One of the last times I spoke in the house I spoke of parasites in the grain trade, and I have been reminded by Major Strange, a prominent grain authority at Winnipeg, that he has never seen any parasites in the grain trade. I never thought that Major Strange would take my statement to mean the employees of the grain companies. Far from it; when I speak of parasites in the grain trade I am talking about the man who has the gambling instinct, the instinct to buy and sell to make easy money, speculating on the grain exchange.
I recognize the research work that has been done by the different companies, but that has nothing to do with speculation on the grain exchange. The man who has that gambling instinct in his blood can go to the horse races or to the greyhound track. I know from experience that when you go to the races you do not hurt the jockey; you do not hurt the racehorse; you only hurt yourself. But if a man starts gambling in the food of a nation, then he is harming others. He is creating false markets and is depriving the farmer of that steady market which should exist for twelve months of the year.
Look at rye to-day. It is a disgrace to Canada that this government ever allowed speculation to continue in rye. I have statistics from the Sanford Evans-statistical service, and if you follow these figures through 1944, 1945 and 1946 you will find that when the farmer was unloading his rye it was always cheaper than when he had no rye to sell.
If the farmer sold his rye when the markets were high he would get a high price, but the market is high only when he has nothing to sell. Moreover, as my hon. friends know, taxes, mortgages, agreements of sale and other expenses generally have to be paid in the fall and the farmer is forced to sell at this time when the price has always been much lower.
It would be interesting to know how many bushels of rye have been sold in 1946-rye that never existed or was never grown. When the grain exchange was asked for this information it did not think it was in the best interests of the people to give it. We can rest assured, however, that the visible supply of rye was sold many times, over and over again.
In conclusion, I do not think I could express my views better than to quote from an editorial in the Western Producer of July 4, 1946:
Public memory is notoriously short, but the farmer we believe retains his longer than the average. He will not yet have forgotten the tragic recurrence of slump and boom which has transformed the basic business of farming into almost a gambling venture. We do not propose to go into particulars here, but in the time-honoured tradition of tile after-dinner speaker, we may be permitted to make a point by recounting an illuminating and absolutely true story. One of the giants of the world grain and milling business was recently discussing the future of wheat. He is a convinced believer in the "open market" and made no bones about it. One of his listeners ventured to suggest that if the grain exchanges were allowed to operate freely at the moment wheat would almost certainly advance sharply. He wondered whether this big operator with huge milling interests would welcome such an advance? He got his answer. "Three dollar wheat," said the operator, "is the quickest and the shortest way to fifty cent wheat."
That remark is one which every farmer should ponder long and deeply.
But why go on? The overwhelming majority of western farmers have, time and again, demonstrated their unanimity on certain vital points. Among them are these: they want the Winnipeg grain exchange erased, blotted out, done away with for all time; they want the wheat board recognized and accepted as a permanent part of the marketing system; and, to take the place of the madly fluctuating "open market", they want a negotiated, stable price fixed from time to time at a level acceptable to the producer

The Budget-Mr. Bryce

and the consumer. These are the truths which the farmer holds to be self-evident and about which, there is no argument.
In one of the last grain, bulletins to come to my desk the editor refers to the so-called farm organizations being cooperatives and not representing the farmers. There are many farmers in the farm organizations who do not belong to the pools or other cooperatives-* I am one of those who do not belong to the pool-but for the grain exchange to come along and claim to represent fifty per cent of the western farmers is too funny for words.
Let the record speak for itself. Since the days of the patrons of industry right up to the present time the grain exchange and private grain trade have fought against every move the farmer has made to improve his condition. Think of the fights that have been put up regarding: (I) The expulsion of the first farmers' grain company from the Winnipeg grain exchange for their announced intention to pay patronage dividends. (2) The lobbying by the grain trade for the discontinuance of the Canadian wheat board in 1920. (3) The bitter campaign of misrepresentation by the grain trade against the wheat pools in 1929 and subsequent years. (4) The violent opposition of the grain trade to the present wheat board established in 1935.
Oh, no, no farmer who has lived on these western plains and produced the grain by the sweat of his brow over the last forty years will ever forget these things. Speculation and gambling in food with two-thirds of of the world hungry and starving cannot and will not be tolerated. The grain exchange is doomed. The writing is on the wall; it is there in large electric lights. Orderly marketing is the modern way.
Mr. Speaker, my last words are, let us remember that in many farm, homes, men and women, regardless of present prosperity, long for the day when stabilization and reasonable security will replace fear of the future.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate I am almost tempted to answer the remarks which I heard around me just before I rose to my feet. One hon. member said that this looks like Caledonia night. I say to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), do not be discouraged. I remember when I came to the house back in 1930. When I made my first speech I was told that there were only two languages permitted in the House of Commons, namely, the French and the English. I can tell the hon. member that since that
[Mr. Bryce. 1
day hon. members have understood, if not by words, at least by gestures, all I really meant to convey.
My first words are to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on the budget which he has just brought down. I wish to compliment him not only on the present budget, but on his handling of the finances of Canada during six strenuous years of war. It has been my good fortune to sit in the house under six finance ministers. I recall each and every one of them, but I have one particularly in mind, who I now understand lives among the mighty in Montreal. I refer to the Hon. Charles Dunning. I well remember him as minister of finance, on being asked to expand the amount given to the old age pensioners, rising in his place and asking, where will the money come from? He is probably remembered to this day as the man who asked that question. The Minister of Finance has answered that question fully, because by his ability and the efforts of his officials he has raised the largest amount of money to be expended throughout the years of war that has ever been raised by any finance minister since confederation. We were disappointed when we heard rumours that the Minister of Finance would, perforce, have to take a holiday. All hon. members who know something of the work of the cabinet ministers realize that there has been no harder worked cabinet minister or one who has burned the midnight oil longer than the present Minister of Finance. However, I was not surprised when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced to the house that he would take advantage of the well earned holiday of the Minister of Finance by asking him to go to Geneva to represent Canada at the Geneva conference. I am not at all surprised at the Prime Minister doing that, because a more able minister he could not have chosen.
Since the Minister of Finance has consented to go to Geneva the country and parliament should have a statement from him on his return and from the Prime Minister on his return from the Paris conference regarding the many conflicting statements which have been appearing in the press in regard to conditions in Europe. I am going to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to a statement accusing UNRRA of a grave charge. I shall ask him to investigate this and other matters as well in connection with UNRRA when he goes to Geneva. On his return I trust that in his official capacity as representing the government he will be able to inform the house just what is going on there. The statement to which I refer appeared in

The Budget-Mr. Reid
the National Home Monthly of Winnipeg, of May, 1946, and was written by Leonard Mosley. The magazine may be found in the reading room. Mr. Mosley writes:
Any afternoon this spring, in the narrow streets behind Omonia square, in Athens, you can see large groups of pinched and ragged urchins slopping miserably about in the mud. All around them piled high on barrows and stalls are the shoes that should be on their bare feet, the coats that should be warming their rieketty bodies, and the tins of food they should be eating. But the shoes cost $160 a pair, the coats $240 each, and the meat, butter or beans $6 a can. Yet Canada and Britain and America paid for all those goods on these black market barrows. They are UNRRA goods sent to this country at our expense to keep these Greek urchins . . . and the story of how they got on to the black market is typical of what happens to UNRRA in a land like this . . .
In the six months which ended last December UXRRA imported into Greece $18,000,000 worth of foodstuffs and another $56,000,000 worth of clothing . . . that, combined with internal resources, should have given every Greek 2,000 calories daily . . . and clothed all who really needed it . . . despite some magnificent work by Canadian, American and British personnel in Greece, the supplies that should have saved the lives of hundreds of people were diverted to the black market or blocked by Greek officials for political reasons.
Then Mr. Mosley goes on to tell the entire shocking story. If these statelnents are true I think it is time we reviewed the entire situation. What is everybody's business is nobody's business. If those conditions exist, in my opinion it would have been far better, and would be better now, if Canada handled the distribution of her own goods. The people of this country have contributed largely to the funds of UNRRA; yet the goods have not reached the people for whom they were intended. Then this writer speaks about surpluses in Denmark. I trust the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) will travel through these countries and, when they come back, tell the people of this country and parliament just what they have actually seen. These statements and letters which have been appearing in fhe newspapers from people who have held high official positions in these countries, are disquieting. Just a few days ago i saw that Right Hon. Anthony Eden in Brita-in had asked where all the wheat was going, and a blue paper brought down in the British House of Commons stated that some twelve million tons of wheat had been made available to Britain and to Europe. Is it any wonder that the people of Britain are beginning to get restless, the people who bore the brunt of battle for six long years and who now have to queue up for bread? It is not due to the fact that Canada has not sent enough supplies, because 83260-21 Si
we have; but if the wheat and other goods are being used to play what are called power politics, we should be informed. I believe parliament should have a complete statement on the return of the Prime Minister and the other two ministers. We also read articles in which it is stated that American wives in Berlin, for instance, can obtain more goods there than can be obtained in the United States. I am not going to take up the time of the house by mentioning all the goods these American women found in Berlin only a month ago, but the article says plenty of butter, plenty of clothing and plenty of other goods can be obtained in Berlin. I do not want to labour the question, but if these statements are true something should be done about it, and if they are not true an official statement should be made by the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of Finance on their return to this country.
Leaving that matter for the moment and coming to the question of dollar parity, may I say that I for one was particularly pleased when the minister announced that our Canadian dollar would be equal in value to the American dollar. As a matter of fact the Canadian dollar is the best dollar in the world to-day. There are people in the United States who for some time have been coming to Canada whenever they wished to send funds to European countries. Why? Because the Canadian dollar is recognized in Europe as the best dollar in the world;'yet for a number of years it has been at a discount in the United States. I happened to be in that country the day it was announced that price ceilings would be lifted, and I took it upon myself to ask both merchants and men on the street how they felt on the matter and if they liked the idea. I also inquired as to their views in regard to the reason for lifting price ceilings. Here are some of the answers I received, not only from merchants but from quite a number of others as well. "The black markets have got out of hand," they said, and they quoted the case of butter as but one example. The ceiling price on butter had been set at around sixty-two cents. You could not get any at that price; but one person said, "Give me $1.25 for each pound, and I will get you all the butter you want." Another person I met said there was a great shortage of nylon stockings, and asked if I knew where they were. I said, no, I did not. "Well," he said, "they are down in Mexico." Apparently higher prices are being obtained in Mexico for many products manufactured in the United States; hence the shortages that have existed in that country for some considerable time.
The Budget-Mr. Reid

There is another matter I should like to mention. I do not know whether we can do anything about it, but I want to draw it to the attention of the minister. For some time past there has been excessive buying by Americans on the Canadian side, of goods which are not obtainable in their own country. Only the other day I had a letter from a dealer in tires, who told me it was impossible now to buy a tire, that for the last two months nearly all available tires have been bought and picked up by United States tourists. It is true that we like to have their money; it sort of balances trade; but, after all, if we are to be kept under strict rationing and price ceilings I believe we should keep our eye on the amount of scarce goods which are being taken across the line out of the country.
That brings me to a thought I had in regard to black markets, and for a moment or two I should like to deal with the accusations that have been made in regard to the black markets in lumber in British Columbia. Before doing so, however, in commenting upon the dollar parity I may say I suppose it all depends whose ox is being gored; but I believe it is best for the general welfare of Canada that this has been done. I am going to mention one or two articles in which we will benefit. We in British Columbia import our gasoline in the form of crude oil. Removal of the ten per cent discount will mean a lower price, unless of course there is a price increase in the United States; but in any event it should mean that we can purchase our crude oil for ten per cent less. Then the cities and municipalities whose bonds are still held in the United States, and on which a ten per cent premium had to be paid, will save considerable money. Money will be saved also on any machinery that must be bought in the United States. I know this change will affect gold .mining. Here again, however, the entire industry of gold mining depends largely upon the fictitious price of $35 an ounce set by the United States; and whatever they do with the price of gold will affect gold mining in Canada far more than bringing our dollar to parity.
What I am a little perturbed about, however, is the great drop in the exchange value of the pound. When the United States dollar was at a premium of ten per cent the British pound was also at a premium of ten per cent; but when the minister announced the removal of the premium, bringing the dollar to parity, the British pound dropped almost out of sight. At least it dropped to $4.02, buying, and $4.04, selling. I suppose this has been done because the British pound in the United States has been set at that price. But that is going to affect us far more than the parity of

our dollar with the United States dollar. Before the war, to a great extent we depended upon Great Britain as a market for our wheat, our lumber and our fish. I do not know about the lumberman, because he is not subsidized, but I do know that the Canadian farmer and the Canadian fisherman will probably not recognize that a change, has taken place, because the government will pay the guaranteed price in Canadian funds. But when it comes to a question of lumber, I am just wondering what will happen to the lumbering industry. How are they going to get along? I know there are those who say, "It will be all the better for us, if no lumber is exported; we shall have more lumber." That may be true for the present, Mr. Speaker, but I am taking a long-range view. Before the war, sixty per cent of the lumber produced in British Columbia was sold on world markets, and we depended upon those world markets to supply us with the money with which to buy millions of dollars worth of goods in the protected markets of Quebec and Ontario.
I hope trade between Great Britain and Canada is encouraged. I hope it will be an incentive for us to buy more British goods; because, unless" <we do, I cannot see, after looking at the trade figures, just how Great Britain is going to continue to trade with this country. That is the way it strikes me, after examining the trade figures from 1939 to the present time.
Coming back to the United States dollar, I have all the trade figures of that country before me, and I know this is only one small aspect of the entire picture of dollar parity. We have an adverse trade balance with the United States of $1,668 million for the calendar years 1939 to 1945. This means in dollar exchange that we paid them over $166 million more than we should have paid them. No explanation has yet been given for the drop in value of the British pound. The value of the British pound was $4.64; it is now placed at $4.02. I wonder what that will mean to our people here, especially if there were no subsidy and no guaranteed price being paid. It would be just a little unfortunate. I remember the days from 1030 to 1935 when the pound went down to S3.63, and I remember the cry which went up from the prairie farmers about the great losses which occurred during those years when we got only $3.63 for each British pound's worth of wheat purchased from Canada.
Mr. ILS-LEY: The pound sterling dropped ten per cent, like the United States dollar. The hon. member's figures are not quite correct.

The Budget-Mr. Reid

speechtext: I thought the British pound was $4.64.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then. I shall have to accept the minister's figures. I know they are correct, or he would not quote them. And, having those figures in view, the outlook is not just as dark as I thought it was.
To come to the question of lumber, the accusation has been made by legion bodies and by other responsible bodies in British Columbia that black markets in lumber are operating extensively. I do not know whether they are or not; but it should be the responsibility of the government to have the matter investigated. Such charges are serious, indeed.
There is no one but must admire the creditable task performed by the minister's department in holding down price ceilings. On July 1 newspapers were appearing in various places stating that rents would go up ten to twenty per cent in the United States, food $250 a year and clothing $100 a year for a family of four. That is only the beginning. I am one who believes implicitly that most lines under the ceiling should remain there until our shelves in Canada are stacked with ample goods for the people who require them and who now have the money to buy them. I support the minister to the utmost in the efforts made by him and his officials to hold down certain price ceilings.
May I offer one criticism, howeker, respecting some of the rental regulations. We in British Columbia feel that the officials are not too kindly disposed to us in that province. I have particularly in mind rental control. All hon. members know something of the scarcity of homes to-day. But in my opinion there are some landlords who are taking a terrific beating during these past six years. The regulations have been such as to prevent many people from opening their homes and taking in those needing housing accommodation. They realize that under present regulations, having taken persons in, it is impossible to have them removed.
It would seem that the rental regulations were made primarily for the eastern and central provinces, and perhaps for the prairies as well. Mind you, I am not advocating that a person should be thrown out indiscriminately, but under the regulations one cafinot evict a tenant between September and April. Well, those who prepared those regulations must have known little about the salubrious climate we have on the Pacific coast. These regulations are for the benefit of climates running to twenty or thirty degrees below zero.
Some of the letters I have received are almost pathetic. For instance, only the other
day I received a letter from a man who had been a veteran of both world wars. He bought a home for his daughter, who married a veteran. But, although he owns that home, do you think he can get the tenant out? No, he cannot. Under the regulations he is not permitted to do so. You cannot force them out, and some of them simply thumb their noses at the landlords. And, as has been suggested to me just now, some are doing that very thing, quite literally.
The argument is made that the regulation is to especially protect ex-service men. I have in my filing cabinet information respecting at least six ex-service men who have bought homes within the past year, but who cannot get into them. The tenants are simply saying that they will not move. I am asking the Minister of Finance to consider this matter seriously, because some of these owners are taking a terrific beating.
For instance, I have one case in mind where the tenant is making six times more money than the landlord.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know of the same kind of case.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The landlord has to do all the repairs, pay the taxes and attend to the general upkeep of the building. Since the war began, the tenant has subdivided and sublet the entire building, and has been drawing five or six times more rental than the owner of the building. I draw this to the attention of the minister. It is all very well just to gloss it over; but these things are doing something to our people; they are doing a great deal of harm, something which will embitter them for many years to come.

speechtext: What would you do about it?

speechtext: There is one thing I would do; I would take these rental appeals out of the hands of lawyer judges. I would get men who had a little more humanity in them, men who were not bench-trained in the law, men who did not cross every "t" and dot every "i".

speechtext: Humanity for the tenant or humanity for the landlord; which do you want?
