subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is a great interrupter; he is one of those who can give it out but who cannot take it. I do not like rude interruptions. I have a speech that I want to deliver and some of the interruptions are almost impertinent.
I should like to come back to the question of lumber. I think the prices board did wrong in lifting the ceiling on the prices of logs:	I can tell the minister the twofold
effect this is having. First, taking the ceiling off the price of logs in British Columbia is forcing the small, independent mill man out of business and is gradually concentrating control in the hands of the large mill man who has his own woods operations. Second, taking the ceiling off has brought up the price of No. 3 logs to a point where it is almost equal to the wholesale price of lumber.
To-day No. 3 logs in the open market cost $25 per 1,000 feet, whereas the wholesale price of lumber is $27 per 1,000 feet. The prices of No. 1 and No. 2 logs are much higher. No. 1 logs, which cost $24.50 per 1,000 feet in 1940 cost $40 per 1,000 feet at the present time. No. 2 logs,, which cost $19.50 per 1,000 feet at that time, are now worth $30 per 1,000 feet. Back in 1940 No. 3 logs cost $14.50 per 1,000 feet and, as I said, they now cost $25.
I am going to suggest to the minister and the government that it is high time some real inquiry took place in regard to the entire lumber situation in British Columbia. On the one hand, wages, the price of logs and prices of material, have gone up, while, on the other hand, there is a group saying to the government, "Do not allow lumber prices to rise." I am not going farther into the question this evening other than to draw the attention of the minister to the seriousness of the situation and suggest that it is high time it was investigated.
Coming back to the budget, I was pleased, and I suppose every hon. member was pleased, to hear the announcement made that farmers and fishermen would now be allowed three years over which to spread their income. That will be of inestimable value to our farmers. In answer to the criticism that this period should be five years, I would reply that the farmer can take any three years he wishes. He can take the next year, the fourth year or the fifth year and spread his income back over any three years. I think the announcement made by the minister will be well received.
I should like to say a word now with regard to what the government has done in the budget m connection with cooperatives. There [Mr. Beid.l
has been a great deal of confused thinking and speaking since the announcement was made, in regard to the taxation of cooperatives and allowing patronage dividends to be free of tax. I listened to one speaker, a member of the C.C.F., who rightly said that cooperatives should be encouraged and that people should be encouraged who endeavour to lift themselves up by their bootstraps. Of course all these people should be helped. I doubt if there is an hon. member in this House of Commons who is not in favour of advancing and helping the cause of the cooperatives.
I am a little surprised, however, at some of the statements that have been made by members of the C.C.F., especially those who spoke so frequently against profits shortly after the inception of their party. It is a well known fact that there are cooperatives which are strictly profit-making organizations, and there is the true cooperative, the one where men band together, profitably to themselves it is true, but not with their eye on getting profits, the kind of profits so glibly connected with free enterprise or the capitalist movement. Under this budget, that organization which is a cooperative in the true sense of the word is actually helped.
I have the honour to represent a constituency in which is located one of the most successful buying cooperatives in Canada. This organization has 2,300 members and has an annual turnover of $2,000,000. They buy wheat and grain from the prairies and they charge just about the same as the other milling associations. Naturally they have a surplus or profit, but that profit is distributed among the members in the form of patronage dividends and so will not be taxable. Where in fairness, therefore, can any charge be made against the Liberal government that they are trying to keep down the cooperatives?
Some people again try to link the cooperatives with socialism. I well remember in the early days of my youth when our family was a member of the Scottish cooperative association, one of the finest in the world. Will any hon. member rise in his place and say that they are not a profit-making organization? They had a regular slogan in those days, "The more you eat, the bigger the dividend." The prices they charged were exactly the same as those charged next door, but with this difference. Instead of one man getting the profits, they were distributed among the members of the cooperative association as patronage dividends. Make no mistake; they are really profits as we know them.
There are cooperatives in this country which are just as capitalistic as any capitalist organization one could name, They are not true

The Budget-Mr. Reid
cooperatives in fact at all. To my mind, the action of the government will clarify the entire situation and at the same time help the true cooperatives.
I should like to deal for a minute or two with income taxation. I suppose the ideal state would be one in which we could carry on our business without the imposition of any taxes at all. However, I would remind hon. members that during the war, when the large budgets were being brought down, the only members who protested against borrowing money were the Social Crediters. We were all willing that the government issue victory bonds and no one rose in his place and said, "Mr. Speaker, I say to the Minister of Finance that we should not borrow; we should pay our war expenditure 100 per cent." The only ones who talked differently were the members of the Social Credit group who were against borrowing money.
To my mind, what the minister has done in this budget is outstanding. Starting with 1943, we had a deficit of over $2,500 million. We issued bonds for that; we borrowed for that deficit and no one was greatly perturbed. In 1944-45 we again had a deficit of over $2,500 million. From 1943 to 1946 the deficits' of this country totalled $7,151,217,000. Now we have this budget showing a deficit for 1946-47 estimated to be not over $300,000,000. In addition, the Minister of Finance tells us that in the following year he expects to be able actually to balance the budget. I think that is sensational, and it is something which we can be justly proud of. I have listened to the wail- of those who say that the income tax is too onerous; but if the bank deposits and the bonds held by the people of this country are any criterion, I am surprised that anyone would squeal about taxation. In 1939 the bank deposits of all individuals amounted to $1,678,363,561. Note what it is to-day? Bank deposits held in the names of individuals are up to $3,305,701,658. Further, take the bonds held by individuals; in the nine victory loans which we have issued successfully under the guidance of the Minister of Finance, they hold $12,355,000,000. As a matter of fact, if everyone agreed that what they own would be given to wipe off the debt we would have no debt left at all. That is a revolutionary idea, I know, but when people talk about a jubilee by wiping off the debt, remember, whether we agree with the idea or not, that there is as much money in the hands of the twelve million people of Canada to-day as would wipe out the dominion debt. When they get up and talk about taxation hurting
I say for numbers of our people this is going too far. The thing just does not make sense.
I have just one word to say on the dominion-provincial conference, and then I will close, because I see I am just about through as far as time is concerned. I am one of those who was greatly disappointed at the lack of results of the conference. I want, however, to make one or two comments regarding the recent offer made by the Minister of Finance to the provinces. I should like to have seen the minister attach to these proposals the suggested social security measures. I think it is a mistake to allow the two central provinces forever to run this country. I say that openly, and I do not think it can be successfully contradicted. I am thinking particularly of the old age pensioners in British Columbia, who were looking for the acceptance by all the provinces of the proposals made at the conference; and I am going to ask the Minister of Finance to think over this point seriously. When the old age pension legislation was put into effect in 1927 the wage level, taking 1939 as 100, stood at 97. To-day the price level stands at 137, forty points up. If $20 were considered enough in 1927, what must the need be to-day, when the wage level has increased forty points? Reference was made by one of the ministers about freezing the cost of living bonus which has been given to civil servants and making it permanent. Well, I am all for it. But I do not know what answer I will give to the old age pensioners of British Columbia who ask me, "Why should these people who are working get more by way of a cost of living bonus than the small amount the government now gives us?" I say to the minister, give the matter of old age pensions some thought, and if he can, revise the proposal to the various provinces, because if he can get seven to agree to his financial proposals with the social security measures which were enunciated included, it will go a long way to bring the other two mto line.
I have only time for one word more. I saw in the paper the other day a statement made by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bracken). It reads:
New offer by the dominion government to deal with the. provinces individually in making new tax agreements substitutes coercion for consultation and brings the danger of "Balkanization" to Canadian relations, in the opinion of John Bracken, Progressive Conservative leader.
In a speech prepared for delivery over a national radio network Wednesday night, Mr. Bracken declared that if he had been in the position of Prime Minister at the recently indefinitely adjourned conference an agreement would have been reached.

The Budget-Mr. White (Hastings)
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that, holding the position he does as leader of the Conservative party and as leader of the official opposition, he should come into this house and tell the house and the country in what particular he would have offered terms to the provinces differing from or better than that of the Minister of Finance. He owes that answer to the country. I leave that suggestion with him.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with reference to the concluding remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I would not presume to speak for my leader, but I will say I am sure that if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) had been in charge of the dominion-provincial conference he would never have held a big club in the manner in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) did over the provinces. I think it is well understood that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance really wanted the conference to fail, in order to get out of many of the social security measures which they had promised and which they knew they could not fulfil.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I deny that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister may deny it, but he will find there are many people in Canada who believe that he and the Prime Minister were looking for an alibi to get out of their obligations.
In regard to the remarks of the hon. member with reference to rent control and rental regulations, I wish to say only a word. The hon. member referred to the manner in which these regulations were administered and suggested that they be taken out of the hands of the county judges. But I would point out to him that the judges did not draw up these regulations; all they can do is to interpret them, and those who practise law will, I think, agree with me when I say that these rental regulations are in many instances, both ridiculous and absurd. After all, what else can one expect when they are drawn up and put into force by this autocratic and bureaucratic wartime prices and trade board.
The hon. member referred to the difficulty of returning veterans who wished to buy a home or to secure rented accommodation. Every member who has had anything to do with them knows the restrictions under which the soldier has to operate. I remember that, speaking in this house some two years ago, I suggested that these rental regulations should be reviewed and that they should not apply to every little hamlet and four corners throughout the country.

The hon. member has just mentioned that many people who in normal circumstances would be willing to rent part of their houses, a flat or a room, when they are advised that once they let a tenant in he is in "for the duration", simply say, no. After all, in many cases one cannot blame them.
I only wish to deal with one item in regard to the budget, and that is the resolution which deals with the amendment to the Succession Duty Act, and which reads:
That rates of tax upon or in respect of any succession upon the death of a person after December 31, 1946, shall be twice the rates presently in force and that the tax paid to the government of any province in respect of the same succession be allowed as a deduction from the tax payable under the Dominion Succession Duty Act up to but not exceeding one-half of the tax otherwise payable under the said act.
In this regard, I should like to refer to certain remarks of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mayhew), as reported in Hansard, at page 3259:
The impression created by editorials and statements appearing in the press is that the dominion has doubled the rate of succession duties that w'ill apply on estates in 1947. How such a gross misstatement of the facts could have been seriously advanced is beyond my comprehension. The dominion's proposal was simply that the rates of duty under the dominion act would be doubled and that any duty paid to a province would be offset against the dominion duty up to one-half the amount of the increased dominion duty. Since existing provincial duties are now generally as high as or higher than one-half the increased dominion duty, in general there will be no increase in total duty under the change.
I would emphasize the last line, that in general there will be no increase in the total duty under the change. In the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, at page 2905 of Hansard there is a forecast of the estimated amount of succession duties to be $24 million as compared with $21 million for the year 1945-46. That is an increase of $3 million for a period of only three months as far as the new rates are concerned, and for a period of twelve months the increase on the same basis would be $12 million. In the same budget speech, at page 2924, the Minister of Finance estimates that the succession duty collected in one full year under the new rate will be from $48 million to $50 million, less whatever amount is allowed for duty. paid to the province.	.
If the succession duties are increased at least $12 million a year, it is hardly - fair or reasonable for the Minister of Finance or the parliamentary assistant to say that there has been no increase. I contend that in the average small estate there will be the full increase of 100 per cent in dominion succession duties

The Budget-Mr. White (Hastings)
after the first of January, 1947, and the parliamentary assistant, at page 3259, gave two examples of how the double increase would work out. Unfortunately, however, he took only two large estates. He took one of $50,000 and one of $2 million, but he made no mention of the average small estate which would be exempt from provincial duty, except for the following remarks which are found at page 3259:
There may also be individual eases where the dominion taxes a succession which the province does not tax or possibly taxes a succession in a manner different from the provincial practice where the duty under the dominion's proposal might be increased. In these cases, however, the increase would normally be relatively small in amount, and would not affect the general statement that the level of succession duties in Canada has not been raised.
That is very plain English; and, coming from the parliamentary assistant, I take it that the Minister of Finance contends that there will be no increase under the dominion succession duty rates except for the remarks about a relatively small amount which would not affect the general statement that the level of succession duties in Canada has not been raised.
I would refer, the minister to the following example. In the province of Ontario, in all estates up to $25,000 which pass to preferred beneficiaries there is no succession duty payable to the province, and in estates passing to those in the collateral class there is no duty up to $10,000. My contention is that in all these estates up to $25,000 that pass to preferred beneficiaries, the heirs are going to be called upon to pay an increase of 100 per cent in succession duty to the Dominion of Canada.
The Minister of Finance and his parliamentary assistant may consider this increase, to use their own language, a relatively small amount, but I would point out that these small estates are the ones least able to bear any increase in succession duty. There may be some justification for taxing large estates; but in my opinion the imposition of succession duties on small estates is only legalized robbery; and I say to the Minister of Finance that if it is his contention that there is to be no increase in dominion succession duties, then he should see that some provision is made whereby this full 100 per cent increase will not apply to any estate which is not taxable in the province.
If I am wrong in my contention that there is a full 100 per cent increase in succession duty rates as I have outlined, I shall be glad if the minister or his parliamentary assistant will correct me. While I have not
the figures before me, I am quite satisfied that it is the average small estate that makes up the bulk of the succession duties collected. The same thing applies to income tax. It is the average small taxpayer who makes up the great bulk of the taxes collected, because only last Friday, at page 3404 of Hansard, to show the enormous amount of income tax paid by the low income tax group, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) said that if the exemption were raised to $1,200 for single men and $2,000 for married men there would be a loss of revenue of some $325 million.
There is the further point that if the Minister of Finance does make an arrangement with a province or all the provinces and the provinces give up their right to collect succession duties, the natural thing that will happen is that the dominion rates will rise, because I recall that during the last dominion-provincial conference the Minister of Finance made a statement to the effect, or at any rate I took the inference from what he said, that if the provinces vacated the field of succession duty the dominion would collect more succession duty taxes than are collected at the present time.
I would also point out to the Minister of Finance and the parliamentary assistant that no mention was made in the budget, as far as succession duties are concerned, about an improved method of making assessments or of speeding up the time in which final releases are granted to estates. The dominion allows only six months for payment of succession duties without payment of interest. The minister knows that in many estates it is very difficult within the six-month period to find ready cash to pay the duty without sacrificing certain assets of the estate. If only six months are allowed for payment of duty I contend that in any estate where the fault is the fault of the department in making the assessment there should be no interest penalty. I think the minister would be probably the first to say that that is only fair and reasonable. I should like to give him an example. In a small estate I filed the required papers with the inspector on October 28, 1944. With the papers I sent a cheque for the estimated duty. The assessment notice from the department was received on May 9, 1946, and it was dated the previous day, a delay of almost eighteen months. The assessment claimed a further payment of $846.14 for duty, plus a penalty of $60.29 for interest. I realize that that amount is small; but I ask the minister in all earnestness, why should this particular estate be penalized in the amount of $60.29 for interest when they

The Budget-Mr. White (Hastings)
had absolutely no control over obtaining the final release? The delay was entirely due to the department not making the assessment.
Further, in all cases where there has been an overpayment of duty no interest is allowed. In Ontario, at least interest is allowed where duty is paid in advance. The same conditions apply to income tax payments. Every hon. member has had many cases and knows of others where the assessments are held up for a long time. In some cases they are years late, and when the assessment is finally received the income taxpayer always finds there is a penalty added. But where the taxpayer has overpaid his tax and after a long delay he does receive a cheque he is not allowed any interest.
I regret that in his budget remarks the minister did not say that the income tax collection method would be overhauled and brought up to date. At page 2923 of Hansard the minister did refer to the necessity of having some change made in the method of appeals. At the present time a taxpayer may have a legitimate claim involving a small amount, but under the present complicated and expensive procedure the average taxpayer would be much farther ahead financially to pay the amount assessed.
In regard to the new appeal court announced by the minister, he said that it would have the power to review the discretionary powers now vested in the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). I suggest that the minister should have no discretionary powers in regard to income tax. There should be one law for everyone and no case should be subject to the discretion of any minister.
The proposed separate board which the minister said is to be set up to advise the minister on the exercise of certain of his discretionary powers-and I emphasize the word "certain"-is far from satisfactory; for, after all, it is only an advisory board and is restricted to advise on certain of his discretionary powers. The minister also referred to the fact that the board was being instructed to explore carefully the possibility of reducing the number of discretions now vested in the minister. Instead of having them review the matter, I would suggest to the minister that he have them all abolished.
While the savings portion of the income tax was abolished on July 1, 1944, the taxpayer who had an income over $3,000, in making his 1945 return, was still obliged to compute the savings portion and then deduct it. So far as the 1946 forms are concerned'- I am referring to form T-7 B, which is the form used for individuals who make more than one payment a year, March, June, Sep-

tember and December-I find that they are still obliged to compute the amount of the savings portion. I would think at this late date that the income tax department would have been able to issue a new schedule of rates in which the savings portion of the tax would have been eliminated.
With reference to the change in the rates of income tax for 1947, I say to the minister that it is unfortunate these rates were not set to apply from July 1, 1946, because he will recall that when changes were made in income tax rates during the war years they applied for the then current year. The reduction he has made is small in view of the statement reported in the press to have been made by his colleague the Minister of National Revenue. Speaking at Pembroke in the spring, he was reported in the press across Canada to have stated or suggested that there would be a reduction of fifty per cent in income tax. If the minister was misquoted I have never seen any denial in the papers.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, this statement has been made on several occasions by hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I did not speak in Pembroke; I did speak in Renfrew on March 11, and I am not responsible for the headlines; they are written by somebody else. The statement which I did make, and which is reported correctly in the Ottawa Journal of Tuesday, March 12, is as follows. I said:
I have no doubt that when parliament meets announcement will be made about bringing down the budget. We have reason to hope that the budget will be sharply reduced. I cannot say how much it will be reduced although some of us hope we can cut our expenditures by fifty per cent. I thihk we can look forward over the year to decreased taxation but this will depend entirely on public opinion. In recent years there has been a growing demand for increased social services, this is a democracy and as such must conform to the views of the people at large. It is up to the people what scale of taxation they wish. If social services are increased levels of taxation will naturally be' higher than without these services.

The Budget-Mr. Moore
There is nothing in the statement which I made, or in the speech which I made, that would justify the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) or other members who have spoken with reference to this matter crediting to me a statement such as he did, and a statement which I had not any occasion to make.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that it is unfortunate the minister waited until after the budget and at this late day to make the correction.
In my opinion the income tax exemptions, which are now 8750 and 551,500, are not sufficient. They should be at least S2.000 for a married person and $1,000 for a single person, with increased allowances for children. No one will dispute the statement that the cost of living has increased from 50 to 100 per cent over 1939; yet a married man with a family is permitted to deduct from his taxable income only $300 per child, while the amount allowed for the wife is also very small. During the war years the average taxpayer was quite prepared and willing to struggle along and pay these excessive taxes; but, now that the war is over, he is looking for some relief. He wants to be able to buy and enjoy some of the luxuries he was denied during the war years. The salaried taxpayers, often referred to as the white-collar class, have been under a decided hardship during the war, and the budget gives them little relief.
The minister has stated, or someone in his behalf has stated, that he needs this enormous income; but it has been very well pointed out by a number of other speakers in this debate that little if any attempt has been made to reduce controllable expenditures, despite the statement just made by the Minister of National Revenue that the government hopes some expenditures may be reduced fifty per cent. It would be interesting if the minister would indicate in the itemized expenditures which departments are being reduced to this extent. The postponement of the reduction until 1947 may have the further effect of reducing consumer goods. When one remembers the enormous production of clothing and mechanical equipment during the war years it is difficult for the average Canadian to understand just why he cannot buy anything he wishes for his home, why he cannot buy a new suit or a new shirt. It is true one can buy plenty of sport shirts at $5 or $10, but the ordinary white shirt just does not exist. Practically every householder is anxious to buy some type of electrical equipment for which he has been waiting for several years, but at
present he has little chance or hope of purchasing an electric stove, a refrigerator or anything of that type. In the province of Ontario the hydro electric power commission has under way a large programme of extending rural lines, but the prospective consumer finds wiring material practically unobtainable, and he is simply out of luck if he tries to purchase electric labour-saving devices. I suggest that the minister review the whole situation, and that the reductions in the corporation tax, the income tax and the excess profits tax be made effective as of July 1, 1946.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell), reading as follows:
This house regrets:
(1)	That the budget does not provide for tax reductions in the calendar year 1946;
(2)	That the budget gives no indication of any serious attempt to eliminate extravagance or effect economies in the cost of government;
(3)	That the policies of the government are discouraging much needed production.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) presented his budget a few days ago. I think we were all impressed by the manner in which he gave the financial picture of the Canadian economy. All sections of the house recognized the effort he put into the preparation of his budget. While, however, we appreciate the sincerity of the minister in dealing with this subject, it was difficult for many of us to see the financial picture of this country in the same bright colours in which it was painted in his statement. It is true, of course, that one must not be too critical at a time when we are entering the reconversion period. The rehabilitation of our servicemen is in itself a problem which will require a great deal of effort and a major plan if our service people are to regain their rightful position in civilian life. The problem of reconversion is another task which will require a great deal of effort. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) has informed us that in a number of industries reconversion has been already completed, but there is still something to be done in this line and until it is completed we cannot consider ourselves on a truly peacetime basis.
This is the first peacetime budget we have experienced in some seven years, and I think it fair to say that the Canadian people were interested to learn what the government intended to do to meet some of the serious problems which have confronted our people for the past few years. I believe perhaps
The Budget-Mr. Moore

the most serious problem with which our people are to-day confronted is that of housing. There can be no question but that the housing problem has put our people in a difficult position. I do not think it can be said that this problem has developed over the last few years. Housing has been a problem in Canada ever since 1930. We have a tremendous lack of housing due entirely to the fact that the people of Canada have not had at any time sufficient money with which to purchase homes for themselves. In this connection I should like to quote from a series of resolutions passed at a convention of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities, dealing with housing and related matters, held in the city of Winnipeg in 1938:
Whereas it is demonstrable that many thousands of Canadian families in the lower income groups, in both urban and rural areas, are today housed in sub-standard, unsafe and unsanitary dwellings . . .
And whereas the vicious environment of such areas counteracts and offsets the constructive influence of education, public health, social service and religion and contributes to vice, delinquency, dependency and excessive mortality and disease, so that sub-standard housing areas are a source of heavy and uneconomic government expenditures . . .
And whereas it can be shown that the basic reason for the existence of such condition lies in the sheer inability ot many Canadian families to pay the economic rent required for adequate and modern housing accommodation, irrespective of periods of prosperity or depression . . .
And the resolution goes on:
And whereas this aspect of the housing problem being of a universal nature has been and is being handled on a national scale in other countries . . .
Now therefore be it resolved that this conference of mayors petition the government of the Dominion of Canada to introduce without delay an adequately assisted plan, aimed specifically at the provision of housing at low costs and low rents.
That was in 1938, approximately a year and a half before world war II broke out. I am not going to say anything about the conditions which developed after the outbreak of war, because we all realize that the government was too busy with other things to deal with housing on a national scale at that time. But I will say that during the war years the condition did not get any better. It got worse, and to-day we are faced with a problem which cannot be described as anything short of a national emergency. In fact, to-day the housing situation is a national calamity, and I think the government should have taken some steps during the present session of this parliament to deal adequately with that situation.
It is certain a great many of us do not fully realize the shortage of houses that exists in this country to-day. According to the Curtis

report, we are short 500,000 homes in this country, and in addition we have another 250,000 which require repair to a greater extent or lesser extent. Other authorities have told us that the veterans returning from Europe alone will need an additional 200,000 homes. This is a situation which calls for action on the part of the government. It is true, of course, that several acts of this parliament have been passed to deal with this situation. The National Housing Act was passed in the late thirties. I think it is fair to say that act has not been able to cope with the situation. It has not been able to solve this housing problem, for the very good reason that the people who do not have homes in this country are those people who do not get a sufficient amount of the national income to permit them to build homes.
A most peculiar situation exists, if one cares to compare the income tax statistics of the country with the housing situation. I have before me a copy of "Taxation Statistics1', issued by the Department of National Revenue. According to this government publication, in 1945 there were about 1,340,000 people in Canada earning $1,800 a year or less. According to statistics issued by civic bodies in various cities, throughout Canada, it requires approximately $150 a month for a family of five to live under decent conditions, and to maintain a decent standard of living. Obviously, if it requires in the neighbourhood of $1,800 a year for a family to live in decency in this country, and if the total income is only $1,800, they are not going tj have sufficient money with which to build homes. That is the crux of the situation to-day.
I have heard many people complain that they have been unable to get assistance, either under the National Housing Act or under the Central Mortgage and Housing corporation, with which to buy homes, for the very good reason that their incomes were not high enough to enable them to take advantage of that legislation. This is particularly true in Manitoba. Many people have mentioned to me that because their yearly wage was in the neighbourhood of $1,600 they were not considered a safe bet on which to lend money for the construction of homes.
As we view these statistics we find that in Canada we are short approximately a million homes, either new construction or homes which should be repaired; and this is about the same number as the number of people who come within these lower income tax brackets.
I submit that if this housing problem is to be solved it can be solved only in one manner, and that is by the government

The Budget-Mr. Moore
taking hold of the situation, the same as it did in the war years. During the war, if we required production for the army, the navy or the air force, the government simply estimated what was needed for the armed forces, acquired the raw materials and went ahead with the production. Early in the war the government found that they had to have additional plant and factory equipment in order to supply the materials of war. They did not consider how much money they had before they went ahead and built those plants. They simply acquired the materials, the man-power and the other essentials, and built the plants and factories required.
I submit the housing problem will not be solved unless we deal with it in a similar manner. This government should set up a crown company, if you like, to deal with the situation. The purpose of that company would be to produce in Canada the building materials necessary to build these homes. It might even be necessary for them to take over large sections of the forested areas of the country and erect sawmills so as to get the necessary Lumber. In those areas of the country where it would not be efficient to build frame buildings, they could go into the production of brick and other materials for the building of homes.
The only difficult problem in this connection would be the production of plumbing equipment. Because of its dependence upon steel production. I admit it would be difficult to produce plumbing equipment in as short a space of time as it would be to produce these other commodities. However, the government should make a start on such a plan as soon as possible. So much for the housing situation.
There is something else which is going to be of some concern to the people of Canada in the very near future. I refer to the growing army of unemployed. The Department of Labour has issued some interesting statistics respecting unemployment in Canada. At present, according to the figures issued by the Department of Labour, we have approximately 210.000 unemployed people in this country. Out of a population of 12,000,000, it is possible that 210,000 unemployed may not be sufficient for us to say that we have an unemployment problem on our hands. But in all fairness I think we must also admit that when we are considering the condition of unemployment there are other factors which should be taken into consideration.
At the present time we have a six-year backlog in civilian production. According to the Department of Reconstruction, a large
number of our industries have already been reconverted to peacetime conditions. Except for the odd strike, and for a shortage of materials in certain places, industry is going all-out to supply products used in civilian life. When this backlog has been overtaken, undoubtedly a number of our plants will shut down and men will be laid off.
The same is true with respect to our markets in Europe. We have sent vast sums of money to be invested in Europe, to enable those people to 'buy Canadian goods. I am not quarrelling with that; I believe it was the only plan to be followed under the circumstances. But we do not want to forget this, that the day is coming when Europe will be reconstructed, when her factories will be rebuilt and when she will be able to supply her own markets with those things she is now getting from Canada and the United States. When this situation obtains it will result in a further shutting down of Canadian factories and further unemployment of Canadian workmen. When such a situation does develop-and it might be within the life of this parliament-we are going to face an unemployment problem with which the government will have to deal.
Personally, I doubt very much if the unemployment problem of the future will be solved under our present economic system. I make that statement with a good many facts to substantiate it. Before the war began, a great deal of our unemployment was due to technological production in industry. We were applying more and more machinery to the production of goods. During the war years, an even greater advancement in technological production took place in the United States and Canada.
According to our war production board which investigated this situation in 1943, we are told that by the middle of this month in 1946, when our industries have been reconverted to peacetime conditions, 3,750 of our plants will have increased their productive capacity by some eighty-six per cent, with an employment of only thirty-three per cent more labour. Reducing those two factors to the same terms, this simply means that we enter the post-war world with plant and factory equipment capable of turning out the same goods which were turned out prior to the war, but with approximately forty per cent less labour.
So long as we can find a market for our production, we are all right; but just as soon as that market becomes restricted we are back again to where we were during the thirties. I venture to suggest that this government should act at the present time to decide what it is going to do to meet a situation of that kind.
I observed during the course of the debate that some hon. members to my right made the
The Budget-Mr. Moore

statement that members of this group were forgetting their application of, socialism to>
our present economy. In other words, they said that we were forgetting our socialist policy and were more or less dealing in Liberal terms. I do not think that statement is quite true. That may appear to them, to be the case, but I think a little consideration of the subject will make our position quite clear.
It seems to me that at the present time, we must try to get as good a deal as possible from the government for the workers and producers of this country. I am' not saying that we are the only ones who are trying to do that, but I think that is the position which private members of parliament should take. Outside of that I do not think there is any solution of these problems under our present system. The Minister of Finance during his budget address told: us that we had to have foreign markets in order to have prosperity in this country. That is true as long as we are going to operate under a system of private, enterprise. But if we continue to operate under that system we shall end up with the conditions that existed in 1929 when foreign markets just did not exist.
How can every country in the world have foreign markets? The system worked splendidly in 'England when it first began the capitalist economy with the use of the steam engine. If the steam engine had stayed in England the system might have continued to work. European countries were importing English goods; but they were not satisfied with merely doing that; they began to import English steam engines. They built up their own capitalist systems and then, they raised tariffs against English goods to preserve their markets. The system spread all over the world, until by 1929 we found that every country was trying to protect its home market for its own manufacturers by raising a tariff against all others.
Where is there a foreign market for goods at the present time except the market that is due entirely to war conditions? It simply does not exist. Prior to the outbreak of the war, the United States could produce automobiles for nearly five worlds the, size of ours, while Canada could produce automobiles more than sufficient for her own market. Where did, the foreign markets exist before the war for those things? They simply did not exist.
As I see it, the only solution of the unemployment problem, if there is one to be found, is government ownership of the means of. production, distribution and exchange in this country.
