speechtext: How does that solve it?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will solve it by doing away with what has caused the situation. It is the profit motive in industry that has caused the situation.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In other words, if you do not want cars they will not make them and sell them to the other workers?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You may think that, but if you have another solution I am quite willing to listen to it. If anyone can tell me how he proposes to solve the unemployment problem I shall be only too glad to listen to him. But I think it should be brought up in this house because from 1930 to 1939 it was not solved and we are doing nothing at the present time to solve our unemployment problem. The things that caused unemployment in 1929 are with us to-day. As soon as we catch up with this backlog of demand for consumer goods we shall be back where we were. Our solution is government ownership of the principal means of production, distribution and exchange, and I make this suggestion in the interests of the Canadian people.
Some believe that that will lead to a dictatorship, but here is something I ehould like to see considered. Irrespective of what government is in power, the tendency is toward government ownership. We see that with our hon. friends across the way.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not think they are a good government.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall not pass an opinion on that. I shall go a little farther back, to 1935 when hon. gentlemen to my right were in power. They introduced legislation which was regarded as being socialistic, and I refer particularly to the Natural Products Marketing Act. I remember reading Hansard at that time and seeing that the Liberals who were in opposition were viciously attacking the government of that day for introducing socialistic measures. I venture to say that when it comes down to the final battle between capitalism and labour those who are now the government will side with the big interests. I hope I am wrong, but I think they will. When it comes to that day, then it will be the group to which I belong which will go into power.
There is something else that should be considered. All those who believe in socialism do not belong to the C.C.F. All those wbo think the C.C.F. may take power in this country do not belong to this movement. I should like to quote what was said by the premier of one of our provinces, a gentleman

The Budget-Mr. Moore
who happens to be a Liberal premier and who expressed himself in no uncertain terms in connection with this matter. Here is what Premier S. S. Garson had to say with regard to the situation in the future when speaking before the Winnipeg board of trade on January 19, 1946, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press; here is what he had to say about what might be done to solve our problems in the future:
Canadian government and Canadian business are operating in a world environment in which in their own interests they must give a better account cf themselves than they did in the 1930's.	At that time we ineptly staggered
through year after year of depression, only to finally achieve pseudo prosperity in war.
If, in peace, we permit ourselves to descend again into depression, while the socialist states make progress toward prosperity, we shall have a hard time to convince the Canadian people that our system of free government and of free enterprise should not be replaced by some other form of government and some other arrangement for the production and distribution of goods and services.
That is the opinion of the premier of Manitoba with respect to this matter, and that is the opinion of a great many other people who are not associated with the movement to which I belong.
I should like to say a word in connection with the dominion-provincial conference. We had several sessions of that conference but they all ended m failure. I do not blame the government for this, because I think they did nearly all they could to make it a success. Nevertheless the problems it was fondly hoped would be dealt with by that conference are still with us. Allow me to deal with just one of those problems, that of labour.
We have a serious labour situation in Canada to-day, due partly to conditions arising out of the war and partly to the fact that we have a federal versus provincial problem in this country. One of the greatest problems confronting labour is due to the fact that there are nine different governments in Canada each controlling its own local labour situation. I submit that the government should seek amendments to the British North America Act so that we could have a national labour code.
The British North America Act was drawn up to meet the needs of a much less complex society than that in which we are living to-day. Great as were the fathers of confederation, in 1867 they could not foresee the needs of the Canadian people in 1946. I think the present government should do all in its power to seek amendments to the British North America Act. One of the first amendments should be the power to establish in this country a national labour code. I am not going to be
dogmatic as to what the provisions of that code are to be, but a number of labour unions have informed me that they would be quite satisfied to accept P.C. 1003 as the basis of a national labour code. It is true, all labour unions are not quite satisfied with the provisions laid down in these regulations, but if they were accepted as the basis of a federal labour code the various labour unions and the government could get together and make it more acceptable to labour in the future. That is they could make amendments to the national labour code from time to time.
One other thing I should like to deal with before closing is in connection with agriculture. Our economy in western Canada is based very largely on agriculture. The war has done a great deal to bring Canadian agriculture to the position which it ought to occupy in our economy. I think it is fair to say that for the first time in the history of Canadian agriculture it has been accorded its rightful position as a national industry. It is the first time that those engaged in farming have received a fair share of the nation's income. If we want proof of that statement we have only to compare the income tax returns of 1935 with those of 1943. In 1935, according to the returns, only 416 farmers in the whole dominion paid income tax and the amount they paid was $24,0S3. But what a different picture the income tax returns for 1943 show. There is a little difference as far as the rate of taxation goes between 1935 and 1943, but the difference in the amount of tax collected is so great that I think it illustrates my point quite clearly. In 1943, going all out to supply a war-ballasted economy, Canadian farmers paid income tax to the tune of $440,212, just under 4,000 farmers paying taxes. It is particularly significant to note the position of Saskatchewan with respect to the payment of income tax in 1943. As I have already stated, in that year the farmers of Canada paid $440,212 to the federal treasury by way of income tax, and Saskatchewan alone paid $215,835, or almost half of this amount. This is a marked improvement over the conditions which existed during the thirties, when you could count on the five fingers of one hand every farmer who paid income tax in the western provinces.
Permit me to deal for a few minutes with income tax as it applies to agriculture. The Canadian farmer has felt during the last few years that he has been unfairly taxed on his farm production, and there is some reason for his assumption in that regard. The producing unit in western Canada is the farm, but the number of people employed in one farm includes more than the head of the household; there may be twc., three or four persons work-
The Budget-Mr. Moore

mg on that farm, and yet the farmer's income is assessed as if it were the income of one individual earning and paying the tax. This has caused considerable concern in the west.
There is another thing which should be gone into. I believe that the income tax branch should attempt to devise a different tax system, one which would apply to Canadian agriculture. At the present time grains are the largest production in western Canada; but the farmer finds, after producing his grain, that his income tax is up to a certain level and, if he accedes to the request of the government to produce such extra products as butter, eggs, live stock and poultry, his income is so increased that he is placed in another income tax bracket, so that when he weighs' his additional labour against his very much increased income tax he is reluctant to produce these extra commodities. Of course it will be difficult to devise a system of income tax which could be fairly applied to agriculture, but if the government wishes to get this extra production of such farm commodities as I have mentioned it should exempt these things from taxation, at least for the time 'being.
As has been said, the economy of western Canada is based upon agriculture. There is practically nothing else to which the people of western Canada can turn. According to the dominion bureau of statistics in 1943 67-5 per cent of the people of Saskatchewan, 42-1 per cent of the people of Alberta, and 56 T per cent of the people of Manitoba were engaged in agriculture. If you average these three you will find that 55-2 per cent of the population of the prairies are so employed. In addition to this, some 13-5 per cent of the population of the prairie provinces are engaged in transportation and trade. This latter group is certain to be affected by any recession in the agricultural industry. In other words, 68-7 of our population in the prairie provinces is dependent to a large extent upon the success of the farmer. There can be little question that the reason for this situation is the rapid development in western Canada after the completion of the first railroad, some seventy years ago. In fact, it was the great farming possibilities of this area which brought about this settlement. The experiences of, the past have 'been such that we should realize the futility of basing the economy of any one section of this country upon a single industry. Western Canadians are anxious to see something done to bring about the decentralization of Canadian industry by the construction of industrial plants throughout the prairie provinces.

The same situation which confronts western Canada also faces the maritimes. The maritime provinces of Canada are largely agricultural. Figures which I have also procured from the dominion bureau of statistics show that the number of people engaged in agriculture in Prince Edward Island is 62-7 per cent; in Nova Scotia, 24 per cent, and in New Brunswick, 34-5 per cent. Averaging the three, we have 40-4 per cent of the population of the maritimes engaged in farming. I have mentioned the maritimes because it seems to me that they suffer from much the same economic circumstances as do we in western Canada.
I know that when you talk about building industries in these sections of the country which are not so well developed as the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec the problem immediately arises, where are you going to get the money; who is going to provide it? I am willing to admit that in the past that was quite a problem. It was so because we were a debtor country. Vast sums of money were invested in this country from Great Britain and the United States. The Canadian National Railways is one example, and our great mining industry is another. But since the war I do not think it can be described as so much of a problem as it was before the' war. Canada to-day is lending large sums of money to other countries. I think it would be a good plan if we decided to develop western Canada and the maritimes by investing in these provinces a certain proportion of the amount of money we are lending abroad.
By doing that we would be creating a market right at home for a small quantity of our production. I submit that if private enterprise fails in the future, as it has failed in the past, to accomplish this long overdue task, the government must go ahead and build industries in those provinces and operate them as public enterprises.
The other day an hon. member, I forget who it was, quoted figures from the James report, which stated that the government would have to provide for an expenditure of over $1,500 million a year to provide full employment in this country. I am not going to deal with that, but I think the government ought to reveal as soon as possible what they intend to do to maintain full employment in Canada This is the time to do it. We do not have a large army of unemployed at the present time, but we should have our plans formulated whereby we shall meet this problem when it does arise, which may be before the present administration concludes its term of office.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Earlier tonight we had a speech from the hon. member

The Budget-Mr. Claxton
for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) which was similar in its main lines to speeches given by a number of members of the Progressive Conservative party. It was similar in that it described a condition in Canada which was gloomy and hopeless, which verged on a description of blue ruin, which spoke of scarcity, of taxes and of everything else that was harmful and sad, and which made me wonder, as I heard those speeches, what country those hon. gentlemen were talking about. Was it Canada, or was it some other country?
I ask this house and the people who follow the proceedings in the house to ask themselves, when they hear such criticisms of our country and of the conduct of its affairs: Is this true of Canada? Are they talking about Canada? Because my impression, from knowing something about conditions here, and something about conditions in other countries throughout the world, is that at the present moment there is no country in all the world where I would rather live than in Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Comparisons are odorous at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are quite willing to stand comparison with any country in any respect. I would like to recall to hon. members the circumstances in which' the budget was brought down. It was brought down on June 27. There was a delay of some days while other business was proceeded with, and in that interval two very significant things happened. Hon. members will agree that one way to test the strength of a country, economically and financially, is to see how its dollar or its money stands up in the markets of the world. During that interval an event of major importance happened, and that is that for the first time since 1939 the Canadian dollar was put at par with the United States dollar. This single fact showed, as does the whole state of our economy to-day, that with the single exception of possibly Switzerland, our Canadian money is the equal or the better of the money of any other country anywhere in the world.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it at par to-day in New York and Buffalo?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is it not? The second event which happened during that interval was that the price control in the United States ceased to operate. At that time I was spending two or three days a week in New York attending sessions, first, of the economic and social council of the united nations, and, then, of the international health conference. As I
travelled backward and forward from New York to Ottawa and from Ottawa to New York, I was in the unique position of being able to appreciate the effect of different methods of price control and, later, of no price control, in dollars and cents. To-day, in consequence of the removal of controls, it is estimated that their prices have advanced by twenty-two per cent since price control was removed some ten days ago; that is assuming that estimate to be correct, by an amount which is equivalent to the total amount by which our own price level has advanced since price control was introduced back in 1941- much more, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) says. That, I think, indicates to hon. members and to the people throughout the country something of the value of the administration which we have had in Canada during that time.
These economic policies did not come about suddenly. It was an action of the government of Canada supported by the Canadian people, but under the leadership of the Minister of Finance, whose record in the field of public finance is unequalled anywhere today. And it was under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of his administration.
At those conferences which I attended to represent the government I met the representatives of other countries, as have many other hon. members, and I think they will agree with me that as we move around and meet the representatives of other countries at such conferences or elsewhere we find them constantly amazed at the miracle of the way in which Canada's economy has been conducted during the war-amazed and full of admiration, admiration not only of the government and of the experts who advise the government but of the people of Canada who have so stoutly supported the administration-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And shown such tolerance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and shown such appreciation and good judgment.
With these preliminary remarks I should like for a moment to survey the scene in Canada, with sober good sense, against the sombre background of a world convulsed by war. We must, in considering our own position, regard it at this time in relation to the whole world situation, and we must also recognize that after six years of war it is not possible to reconvert and recover completely in nine months.
In making the statements which will follow, I do so on the best statistical information available to me, and I believe I can support
34S0
The Budget-Mr. Claxton

every one of them. However, I will make those statements boldly andi baldly, and) I think they will stand in contrast with the statements made by the members of the Progressive party and other parties in the house who have taken such a gloomy view.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You mean the Progressive Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, the Progressive Conservative party; I am sorry. As far as possible I should like hon. members to allow me to finish these statements and afterwards I hope to substantiate them as far as there is time.
1.	The production of peacetime goods in Canada is at an all-time high.
2.	We are employing 629,000 more people than in 1939, more people than ever before in peace time.
3.	The Canadian farmers and wage-earners are getting more money than ever before in peace time.
4.	We have to-day the highest production, the highest employment and the highest national income we ever had in Canada in peace time.
5.	The savings of individual Canadians have tripled since 1939 and are at an all-time high. On the other side, debts shown by thirty lending companies alone have been reduced from $169 million to $66 million between the years 1937 and 1945, and it is estimated that during the last six years the total farm debt has been reduced by something over $400 million.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about the national ddbt?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member is still playing poker.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then 6. The ratio of net debt charges to the national income has increased since 1938 less than the United States or in the United Kingdom. I think this is one of the most objective and important evidences of the excellent way in which the economy has been managed.
7.	The rates of cuts in taxes from: their wartime high are. greater in Canada than in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia or New Zealand.
8.	Tax exemptions in Canada are higher for both single and. married taxpayers than in the countries where they have labour governments, higher than in the United Kingdom, higher than in Australia, even after the cut announced Friday, or in New Zealand; they are also higher than in the United States, and with the further exemptions

which will be made effective from January 1, 1947, they will be very much higher than in those countries.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I ask not to be interrupted just now, if the hon. member does not mind until later.
9.	Prices have been more effectively controlled than in any country.
10.	Canadian money is as strong as that . of any country which fought in the war.
11.	The Canadian government has fewer civil servants per capita than the governments of either the United Kingdom or the United States.
12.	Repatriation and demobilization have proceeded expeditiously and smoothly, more rapidly, more smoothly and more successfully than, I believe, any one in 'Canada ever anticipated would be possible.
13.	Canada's veterans' legislation leads the world.
14.	Canada's work in international cooperation has given her a reputation second to no country in the field.
15.	Never before has Canada's reputation for sound progressive government and for successful management of her economy stood so high among other nations.
I shall now be glad if the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) would put the question she wanted to put to me before.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I decided to put it in my
speech.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is a statement of the facts which we should bear in mind in considering the budget and in considering the position of Canada. It should not be thought for a moment that, because we are in so favourable a position, everything is going to go swimmingly for us. We have managed to achieve that position only because we have had a policy throughout the war of paying for as much as we could as we went along and of keeping up the value of our money. We shall continue to enjoy that position only if we continue to have similarly sound policies.
Broadly speaking, there are three conditions for prosperity in Canada. The first is a satisfactory arrangement with the provinces; the second, cooperation between labour and management with government so that we can keep on working and maintain and increase production; and third, the establishment of conditions abroad in which trade can be restored and expanded on a two-way paying basis. Provided that these three conditions

The Budget-Mr. Claxton
are satisfied, we can look forward to the future of Canada with confidence, based on the experience we have had in the past.
In the amendments proposed by the Progressive Conservative party and by the C.C.P. party there are some points on which I should like to make brief observations in so far as time permits. The Progressive Conservative amendment regretted first:
That the budget does not provide for tax reductions in the calendar year 1946.
There we have a revealing statement by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). Referring to the proposed tax reductions he said, as reported at page 3213 of Hansard'.
And, indeed the individual taxpayer will not find any change in his situation until he begins to make out his tax return early in 1948.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario makes it plain that he is thinking of just one class of taxpayers, the smallest class in number, namely, the class who make out their returns and pay their taxes at the end of the fiscal year, and not the great class of taxpayers who have the cut now in force through this year, 1946, month by month, week by week, as they pay their tax in instalments and who recognize that there has been a cut of sixteen per cent.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do they not all make out their returns in the spring.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They appreciate it now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they get and appreciate the reduction now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members may look at the figures which I would give in detail if I had the time. As I have said, the tax reductions from the wartime peak already in force in Canada are greater than those in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, or the United States.
I come to the next point in the amendment:
That the budget gives no indication of any serious attempt to eliminate extravagance or effect economies in the cost of government.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member is agreeing with himself. I am reading his amendment.
In his fine speech on Friday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) showed the house the full range of expenditures over which this or any other government would have control at the present time. It came dowm to a figure of S62 million more than the expenditures in 1939. That is the increase in the controllable expenditures on which this
great cry of economy can operate. I think I can speak for every member of the government when I say that we are continuously alive to the need for economy. Over the past year the Minister of Finance has been supported in his efforts, which I can assure the house have been strong, to secure the application of the most rigid standards of economy in every department.
In that connection, I should like to deal for a moment with the situation concerning the civil service of Canada. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario quoted a figure of 150,000 civil servants, and then said there had been a reduction of only some 900 from that peak figure. I am not at all sure how his figure of
150.000	is made up. The figure given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), in reply to a question in this house on May 6 of this year, was 116,362, but obviously there must be some explanation for the discrepancy, and I assume the figure of
150.000	may be correct.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was taken from a government return.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Apparently there were two returns covering two answers to two sets of questions, which differed because of the way the questions were put-the returns are responsive to the questions. The figure of 150,000 is, I assume, larger than the figure of 116,362, because it includes employees of government agencies and also a considerable number of casual employees. Certainly in the case of the Department of National Health and Welfare, with which I am familiar, it includes all casual employees. Assuming the figure to be 150,000, let us, for purposes of comparison, contrast it with the figures for civil servants in other comparable countries. In the United Kingdom, for example, a command paper handed down in June, 1946, gave the strength of the civil service, as of April 1, 1946, at 695,950, and contrasted it with the picture for the same group of employees as at January 1, 1946. Those figures showed an increase of some
5.000	employees during that time, with an increase in every civil department wdth the exception of three, and it was explained in the return that these increases came about because the government was beginning to get back to normal conditions; they were having to restore peacetime services and make up the differences caused by six years of war. The United States figures showed a total of 2.961,000, or an even larger per capita number of civil servants. The figure for federal government civil servants alone in the United States was 2-12 per hundred of population, whereas the English figure was 1-53 and the Canadian figure,
The Budget-Mr. Claxton

assuming a civil service of 150,000, would be 1-24. In other words, on the basis of the figures I have given, the Canadian figure was considerably lower than either the English or United States figures on a per capita basis. One would expect that a country whose density of population is much less than that of either the United Kingdom or the United States would need more, civil servants to maintain its services; yet the differences are as I have described. them to be.
In talking about economies as applied to the civil service, it would be interesting to leam from, hon. gentlemen opposite who have been so critical whether they regard the rates of pay of civil servants as too high. My impression, and certainly every criticism I get, is that they are too low, not possibly in every range but as a general picture. I can assure hon. members that for every suggestion I have ever heard that the rates are too high I have heard a thousand that they are too low; and I must say I think every minister has been subjected to the most continuous pressure to increase the rates of pay. We now come to the second element. Are there too many of them? There may be. in certain departments, and it requires some time in a large organization to make changes as we turn from a wartime to a peacetime basis. My experience is that a considerable group of civil servants are overworked, and, that there is considerable understaffing in some departments. I do not know of any case where the opposite is true and where the situation when brought to the attention of responsible officers is not dealt with as promptly as is possible. Hon. gentlemen may be surprised to learn that at the present time there is a shortage of stenographers, trained clerks, statisticians, economists and almost every other kind of trained worker that one would want in a government service. So that there is no difficulty about transfers or anything of the kind. There just are not enough qualified people available to do the jobs that have to be done at this time.
If I am right in what I say about wages and about the size of the staff, the only thing left which may be cut is whether or not we are giving, more sendees than the people of Canada want and are willing to pay for. That is the only other element in the picture. My experience, as I have handled estimates on two occasions and have heard other ministers handle them for some years, is that you never receive a suggestion that you cut down a service. It is rather the reverse. From one hon. member opposite after another you get suggestions for this additional service and that

additional service; for more social security and more things that cost money in quantities totally beyond the most extreme suggestions of any savings that could be effected. That is the sort of thing which sometimes leads one to become a little irritated, perhaps, in the face of this constant talk about extravagance, without any particularization that can be supported, while all the time we are faced with additional demands for additional services, not only from every part of the house but from every part of the country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not come from this corner.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, doesn't it? I'll say it does.
Mr. BLACKMORE; But we show you how to pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: From that corner we have had suggestions for additional old age pensions that would cost $850,000,000 a year.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but we show you how to pay for them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not to the satisfaction of anyone in -this or any other country. That is the situation in regard to the civil service. Then we get on to the other things, such as the purchase of materials. I have not heard any hon. member opposite or any people throughout Canada say the federal government pays too much for materials or for supplies or for office space. On all sides I hear criticism that we are too tough a bargainer, so much so that sometimes we are charged with being unfair. I can assure the house that the requests for concessions being made here, or being made there, come just as often from hon. members opposite as they do from members of this party-and probably a good deal more often. That is, I think, a just appreciation of the situation.
Yet we have suggestions that there should be cuts here and cuts there, without any specification; and then at the same time increased demands for social services. We are told we should stop deficit financing-a point made at great length by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. How could we stop deficit financing if at the same time we carried out his suggestions for increased reductions in taxes, and increased interest rates? Why, he would get us into a spiral there that works out exactly the opposite.
Suggestions involving additional expenditures which have been made in the house are being totalled by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott); he says he has someone working on it. Additional expenditures suggested by hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party alone, during this session,

The Budget-Mr. Claxton
would total far more than the largest possible sum that anyone could possibly raise by additional taxation at this time-and that would be just keeping the deficit where it is.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Could the Minister of National Health make a statement as to the requests which have been made to various ministers by members of his own party?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I can, for my department: it is an additional $50 million.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman) was asking for the total of suggestions from hon. members in this party, as compared with those from the Progressive Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, I thought it was a request for information respecting additional expenditures suggested by the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now, as to this question of economy-and it is an important one. Of course it is. We must be eternally vigilant, and we look to hon. members in the opposition to assist us in that vigilance. We look to the public to assist and to support the government in cutting out every possible wasteful expenditure. Of course we must do that. And having done that, as we try to do, then also give us some support when we are faced with requests for things which would cost far more than any possible saving could effect.
With regard to an item in which I am directly interested, namely the administration of family allowances, we have just completed a year of that administration. Our estimates, made before we ever began operations, and based upon the best experience here and elsewhere in respect of similar operations, have been bettered in every respect.
In the last year I believe there have been just three criticisms in the House of Commons made with respect to the administration of family allowances, and I should like to say just a word in reply to each of those. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Gariepy), speaking on Friday, said that there have been some delays in attending to correspondence, and he suggested the establishment of an office in Three Rivers. We have considered the question of opening local offices; indeed that point was considered long before the administration was set up. It was felt it would be much wiser to try to administer the whole operation from offices located at provincial capitals. By and large this has worked successfully, as hon. members from all parts of the house in other debates have been good enough to testify. So far we have seen no reason to open a large number of local offices. It may be
that, in one or two centres in Canada, we shall open inquiry offices, but we hope that those will be kept to a minimum.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram), speaking on the same day, referred in critical terms to the fact that he had not been able to get information he wanted about family allowance administration, and added on this rather sweeping statement:
I find it difficult to get true and honest statements from the government on governmental expenditures. [DOT]
The statement given by the Department of National Health and Welfare in reply to his question was completely accurate. It showed the cost of administration of family allowances to the department for the first six months of operation. It is completely in accord with the statement I later made in the house, and there is nothing about it to explain or to correct. In so far as this department is concerned, the hon. member's statement is not accurate. Figures on expenditures in connection with the operation of family allowances have been given by me in various forms in discussion of the estimates, when we gave the actual costs for the fiscal year. Also I gave estimates showing the cost to every department of the federal government of family allowance administration. We believe we shall keep well within those costs, and hope that hon. members will assist us in doing so.
The third point was made by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, as reported at page 2981 of Hansard for June 27, where he made reference to a subject which had been discussed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) when my estimates were before the committee. Reference was made to our estimate of $300,000 for investigation, where we had spent only $6,000 in the last fiscal year. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was good enough to say that this was no doubt due to the fact that this was partly-"partly"; I draw attention to that word-a new expenditure.
Well, the word "partly" there is put no doubt in an effort to be fair. But I should explain to the house that the "partly" is just about one-fiftieth right. In other words, to the extent of forty-nine fiftieths, or more, this was a new expenditure. The expenditure of $6,000 made in the fiscal year 1945-46 was for one province, representing one-twentieth of the population for three months, or for one-quarter of th$ year. Therefore the amount of the expenditure of $6,000 or thereabouts was about, let us say, one-fiftieth, one-sixtieth, or perhaps one-eightieth of what would be required for the full year. And on that our estimate was based.
The Budget-Mr. Claxton

speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer that when the estimates are being, considered. But it is very little more than at the rate I mentioned before, because of the difficulty of having arrangements established, as I have said.
There is one other matter I should like to -mention before I close, and- that is the speech made by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party over the network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on July 10. In that speech he referred to the budget of this year, and then said:
And in additionwe are being asked by the government-
-to go into debt another thousand million dollars-what for? Not to buy things for ourselves-bu-t-think of it-to pay for our own exports to ship away to other countries.
Mr. Speaker, if I may say so, this is a most extraordinary statement to come from the leader of the Progressive Conservative party. Does this mean that he is opposed to the credits to the United Kingdom and to the other countries to which we are lending money or advancing cerdits in order to enable them to establish themselves and put themselves back in a condition where: they can buy our goods? If it means that, why was that statement made over the air when just five days before a bill to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act was introduced in this house and received the support of the Conservative party? The facts regarding export credits were given to the house, and that amendment, like the bill last year, was carried without division, with the full support of the Progressive Con-
servative party. Was that speech given to cast some reflection upon the use of money for this purpose? Was it intended to have some effect outside the house which could not be sought inside the house? It would be interesting indeed to have this statement fully explained in the light of the support given, by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario for example, and by others to this whole field of assistance by means of this legislation. Where does the Progressive Conservative party stand?
The leader of the opposition ends up with a statement about the dominion-provincial conference when he said:
There are two dangers inherent in this method. The first is that it is a Balkanization procedure.
I should like to ask: Who is being coerced by this procedure? An offer has been made to the provinces. That offer is based on the original proposals first put before the provinces on August 9, 1945, discussed during four separate sittings of the dominion-provincial conference, worked over by the economic committee, discussed at the final sessions between April 29 and May 3, modified repeatedly to the advantage of the provinces and now put before them. Why was that done? It was essential that certain provinces at least know what they could expect. They were given this opportunity without coercion, without any Balkanizing.
I venture to say that it is a wider and broader proposal that even the leader of the opposition envisaged when he so stoutly fought for the province of Manitoba and for a general arrangement between the dominion and the provinces in 1941. I am sure the leader of the opposition would not object to the federal government agreeing with the province of Manitoba or any other province on those terms. If so, It would be most interesting indeed to find out on what terms. It is a remarkable thing that during all the time these proposals have been before the provinces and before the country there has not been any adverse criticism: so far as we know by any federal party. The only alternative proposal put forward and seriously discussed at all was that put forward by the province of Ontario, the details and full weight of which we learned only two days before the conference adjourned.
As I said, I submit that there are three conditions which must be satisfied if the people of Canada are to have the prosperity I believe they could have. First, we must have a satisfactory arrangement with the provinces. Having worked hard at these dominion-provincial arrangements for three

Immigration
years, like everyone else I hoped that it would be possible on the basis of these terms to arrive at an agreement which would be in, the interests not only of the provinces and of the dominion but of the people of Canada as a whole. Here I should say a word in reply to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). If there is anything unconstitutional in these arrangements, then it is strange because we have been paying subsidies to the provinces since 1867, and surely that is legal. Second, we have been working under a tax agreement similar to that proposed since 1941.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is there any reason why a similar arrangement should not be continued by agreement if the parties are willing to agree? We have never failed to carry out any agreement that has been made with the provinces or with any country, and we believe we should be able to rely on them to do the same.
Second, I suggested that our prosperity depends upon the cooperation of management and labour with government in working out conditions under which it is possible to carry on work. Third, the prosperity of Canada depends, as we all know, upon our establishing through collaboration with other nations, conditions abroad under which we can have prosperity at home. Those conditions are not impossible; they depend on good will here and good will abroad. I believe that all hon. members, as well as all the people of Canada, above everything else want us to work together to construct out of the world in which we find ourselves that better world we know we can build.
